q: What is Lightning Web Components and why is it built on web standards?
alt: What is LWC?
Explain Lightning Web Components in simple words
Why did Salesforce move from Aura to LWC?
what is l w c framework
a: LWC is what I'd use for all new UI work. Lightning Web Components is Salesforce's modern UI framework, where you build components with standard HTML, modern JavaScript and CSS. Instead of a proprietary framework layer like Aura, LWC uses what the browser already gives us: custom elements, shadow DOM, ES modules, templates and events. Because the browser does most of the heavy lifting natively, components load and render faster, and the code looks like normal web development, so skills carry over. For example, a JavaScript developer who has never touched Salesforce can read an LWC class on day one, because it's just an ES module exporting a class. Salesforce only adds a thin layer on top for things like security, base Lightning components, Lightning Data Service and the wire service. And LWC and Aura can live on the same page, and an LWC can sit inside an Aura component, but not the other way round. That's also why hiring and onboarding are easier, since general web skills carry straight over.
points: Built on web standards: custom elements, shadow DOM, ES modules
Faster than Aura because the browser does most of the work
Thin Salesforce layer: base components, LDS, wire service, security
LWC can be nested inside Aura, not the other way round

q: What files make up a Lightning Web Component bundle?
alt: What is inside an LWC folder?
Which files are mandatory in an LWC?
What is the js-meta.xml file used for?
lwc bundle structure
a: Simply put, an LWC bundle is a folder named after the component, and normally it has an HTML template, a JavaScript file and a js-meta.xml configuration file. The JavaScript file is required, because it defines the class that extends LightningElement. The HTML file is needed for any component that renders UI, but a service-style module can skip it. The js-meta.xml holds the API version, whether the component is exposed, and its targets, like record page, app page, flow screen or Experience Builder, plus design properties. So for a component called accountCard, I'd have accountCard.js, accountCard.html and accountCard.js-meta.xml inside an accountCard folder. Optional files are a CSS file for scoped styles, an SVG icon for App Builder, and a __tests__ folder for Jest tests. On my teams, that __tests__ folder isn't optional for anything with real logic.
points: componentName.js is required and extends LightningElement

q: Explain the LWC lifecycle hooks and the order in which they run.
alt: What are lifecycle hooks in LWC?
Order of constructor, connectedCallback and renderedCallback in parent and child
Tell me the life cycle of a lightning web component
what runs first connected callback or rendered callback
a: There are five hooks, and the order matters most when parents and children depend on each other. LWC gives us five lifecycle hooks: constructor, connectedCallback, renderedCallback, disconnectedCallback and errorCallback. The constructor runs when the component is created. I have to call super() first, and I don't touch child elements or public properties there. connectedCallback runs when the component is inserted into the DOM, so that's where I load data or subscribe to message channels. renderedCallback runs after every render. disconnectedCallback runs when the component is removed, so I clean up listeners and subscriptions there. errorCallback catches errors from child components. The flow is top-down for creation and bottom-up for rendering. So with a parent accountList and a child accountRow, it goes: parent constructor, parent connectedCallback, child constructor, child connectedCallback, child renderedCallback, and only then the parent renderedCallback.
points: constructor: call super() first, no DOM or public property access
renderedCallback: after every render, child before parent
disconnectedCallback: cleanup; errorCallback: catches descendant errors

q: What is the difference between connectedCallback and renderedCallback, and when would you use each?
alt: connectedCallback vs renderedCallback
Where should I make my Apex call, connected or rendered callback?
Can I access DOM elements in connectedCallback?
when to use rendered callback in lwc
a: connectedCallback is for setup, renderedCallback is for DOM work, and I keep the second one rare. connectedCallback fires once each time the component is inserted into the DOM, before it renders. So I use it for initialization: reading public properties, calling Apex imperatively, or subscribing to Lightning Message Service. The template elements aren't available there yet. renderedCallback fires after every render, including re-renders caused by reactive changes, so the DOM is available. I use it rarely. A typical case is a third-party chart library that needs a real DOM node to draw into. I initialize it in renderedCallback, and I guard it with a flag like chartInitialized so it only runs once, not on every re-render. One more gotcha: connectedCallback can run more than once if the component is removed and re-inserted, so I don't assume it only ever fires one time. Any renderedCallback without a guard flag gets a question from me in code review.
points: connectedCallback: before render, DOM not ready, good for data loading
renderedCallback: after each render, DOM ready
Guard renderedCallback with a flag to avoid repeated work

q: My component goes into an infinite rendering loop. What could cause that and how do you fix it?
alt: Why does renderedCallback keep firing again and again?
LWC infinite loop in renderedCallback
Component keeps re-rendering, how to debug
maximum call stack in lwc rendered callback
a: Almost always, someone is updating a reactive property inside renderedCallback. Changing a field the template uses triggers another render, which calls renderedCallback again, and it loops. Say renderedCallback does this.columns = buildColumns(), and buildColumns returns a new array every time. Each render assigns a new value, which causes another render, forever. A similar loop happens when a getter used in the template changes state, or when a setter on an @api property dispatches an event that makes the parent push a new value back. To fix it, I move data changes out of renderedCallback into connectedCallback, wire handlers or event handlers. If I really need renderedCallback, I use a non-rendered flag so the logic runs only once, and I compare old and new values before assigning, so I never assign a value that hasn't actually changed. This is one pattern I specifically scan for when I review LWC changes.
points: Never set template-bound fields unconditionally in renderedCallback
Use a hasRendered flag or compare values before assigning
Getters should be pure, no side effects

q: How does errorCallback work in LWC?
alt: What is an error boundary in Lightning Web Components?
How do I catch errors from child components in LWC?
Explain errorCallback with an example
error call back lwc
a: I use errorCallback to build error boundaries, so one bad widget can't take down a page. It's a lifecycle hook that lets a parent act as an error boundary. It gets two arguments, the error and the component stack. It catches errors thrown in descendant components, in their lifecycle hooks, or in event handlers declared in their templates. It doesn't catch errors from the component itself. And it doesn't catch errors in asynchronous code, like a promise rejection from an Apex call, which I still handle with try/catch or .catch. What I usually do is wrap risky children in a small boundary component. Say a page has five child widgets and one of them throws in its connectedCallback. The boundary's errorCallback catches it, logs it, and shows a friendly "this section couldn't load" message, so one broken child doesn't blank out the whole page. I'd rather the team share one boundary component than each person writing their own.
points: Catches errors from descendants, not from itself
Async errors still need try/catch or .catch

q: What are the decorators in LWC and what does each one do?
alt: Explain @api, @track and @wire
What decorators are available in Lightning Web Components?
Difference between api track and wire decorator
at the rate api track wire
a: LWC has three decorators: @api, @track and @wire. @api makes a property or method public, so a parent component, App Builder or a flow can set it. It's reactive, so changes from the parent re-render the child. Common examples are recordId and objectApiName on record pages. @track makes the framework watch changes inside a plain object or array, not just reassignment. Since Spring '20, all class fields are reactive by default, so @track is only needed for deep mutation. @wire connects a property or function to a wire adapter, like an Apex method or getRecord. The framework provisions data and error to it automatically and re-fetches when a reactive parameter changes. So on a record page, I mark recordId with @api, wire getRecord with '$recordId', and the component loads the record by itself whenever that Id changes. In review, I also ask whether each @api property really needs to be public, because every one is a contract other components depend on.
points: @api: public, set by parent or builder, reactive
@track: deep observation of objects and arrays only
@wire: declarative data from Apex or LDS adapters
All fields are reactive on reassignment without any decorator

q: Is @track still needed in LWC? Explain the reactivity rules.
alt: When do I still need the track decorator?
How does reactivity work in Lightning Web Components?
Are all fields reactive in LWC?
do we need at track anymore
a: Mostly no, and on my teams we prefer reassignment over @track. All fields are reactive, so if I reassign a field that's used in the template, or in a getter the template uses, the component re-renders. What the framework doesn't see by default is a mutation inside an object or array, like pushing to an array or changing one property of an object. Say I have this.filters = { status: 'Open' } and then I do this.filters.status = 'Closed'. Without @track, the UI won't update. So I either decorate the field with @track, or, which I prefer, I assign a new copy with the spread operator: this.filters = { ...this.filters, status: 'Closed' }. Even @track doesn't watch Date, Set or Map internals, so for those I always reassign. And wired data is read-only, so I clone it before changing it.
points: Reassignment of any field triggers re-render
Mutation of object/array props needs @track or a new copy
@track ignores Date, Set and Map internals

q: I updated a property on wired data and got an error, or the UI did not refresh. Why?
alt: Cannot assign to read only property in LWC wire data
Why can't I modify data returned from @wire?
UI not updating after I change an array element in LWC
proxy read only error lwc
a: That's the read-only rule on wired data, and the fix is to copy before you change. Data provisioned by @wire is frozen, so any attempt to change it, such as adding a computed field for a datatable, throws a read-only error. The fix is to make a shallow copy first and work on the copy. The second common reason the UI does not refresh is mutating an array or object in place, for example this.rows[0].Name = 'X', or this.rows.push(row). The framework only reacts to reassignment, so I build a new array with map or spread and assign it back. I also check that the field is actually referenced in the template or in a getter, because changes to unused fields never cause a re-render. These two mistakes are common enough that I cover them when new developers join the team.
points: Wired data is read-only: clone before modifying
In-place mutation does not re-render without @track

q: Can a child component change the value of an @api property passed from its parent?
alt: Should I modify a public property inside the child?
Is @api property read-only in child component?
Child wants to change data that parent passed down, what to do?
can child update api variable
a: No, and that's a rule I hold the team to: a child should treat @api properties as owned by the parent. If the parent passes an object or array, it's read-only in the child, and trying to mutate it throws an error. Even for primitives, changing it in the child creates a mismatch, because the parent will overwrite it the next time it re-renders. The clean pattern is one-way data flow: data goes down through @api properties, and changes go up through custom events. Say a parent passes a quantity of 5 to a child quantity picker. When the user clicks plus, the child doesn't set quantity to 6 itself. It dispatches an event with 6, the parent updates its own field, and 6 flows back down. If the child only needs a local editable version, it copies the value into a private field.
points: Data down via @api, changes up via events
Objects passed from parent are read-only in child
Copy into a private field for local edits

q: How do you call a method on a child component from the parent?
alt: Parent to child method call in LWC
How to expose a public method in LWC?
How do I invoke a child function from parent component?
call child component function from parent lwc
a: I'd expose the method with @api and call it through a reference. I decorate the method in the child with @api, which makes it public. Then in the parent I get a reference to the child element, using lwc:ref or this.template.querySelector, and call the method directly. This is useful for actions like reset, refresh or validate, where the parent tells the child to do something. For example, a search page has a Clear button. The child filter panel has an @api reset method, and the parent's click handler calls this.refs.filters.reset(). The gotcha is timing. I only call it after the child has rendered, so from an event handler or renderedCallback, not from the constructor or connectedCallback. Public methods can also return values or promises. I keep these for commands like reset or validate, and send data down through properties, so the parent-child contract stays easy to follow.
points: @api on the child method makes it public
Get the child with lwc:ref or template.querySelector
Call only after render, e.g. in a click handler

q: How does the wire service work in LWC? Give an example.
alt: Explain @wire with an Apex method
What is wire adapter?
How does wire get data reactively?
how to use wire with record id
a: The wire service is my default for reading data. It's a reactive, declarative way to get data. I decorate a property or function with @wire and give it an adapter, like an Apex method marked cacheable=true or an LDS adapter like getRecord, plus a config object. When a parameter is prefixed with a dollar sign, like '$recordId', it becomes reactive, so when that value changes, the wire calls the adapter again. The framework provisions an object with data and error. For example, I wire a getContacts Apex method with accountId set to '$recordId'. On an Account page it loads that Account's Contacts, and if the recordId changes, it reloads by itself. Wiring to a property is simplest. Wiring to a function lets me process the result, like cloning it or handling errors. And wire runs when the component loads, it doesn't wait for a user action.
points: Wire to a property or a function

q: When do you use @wire versus calling Apex imperatively?
alt: Wire vs imperative Apex call
Difference between wire method and imperative method in LWC
Why would you call Apex imperatively?
wire or imperative which is better
a: My rule of thumb is wire for reads, imperative for actions. I use @wire for reading data that should load automatically and stay reactive to parameters, like records related to the current recordId. It's declarative, uses the client cache, and needs the Apex method to be cacheable=true, which means no DML. I use imperative calls when I need control over timing, like on a button click, when the method does DML or isn't cacheable, when I need to chain calls in order, or when I want to call it conditionally. For example, showing an Account's open Cases is a wire. A "Close all Cases" button that updates them is an imperative call. Imperative calls return a promise, so I use async/await with try/catch. One trade-off: refreshApex only works with wired results, so with imperative calls I simply call the method again.
points: Imperative: on demand, DML allowed, ordering control
Imperative returns a promise; refreshApex only for wire

q: What does @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true) do and what are its restrictions?
alt: Why does wire need cacheable true?
Can a cacheable method do DML?
Explain client-side caching of Apex in LWC
cacheable equals true meaning
a: I mark a method cacheable when it's a pure read, but I plan the refresh story at the same time. cacheable=true tells the framework the method is a read-only query, so its response can be stored in the Lightning client cache and reused for identical calls with the same parameters. It's required for @wire, and it helps performance because repeat calls can be served from the cache. The restriction is that the method can't do DML. If it tries, it throws an error. The flip side of caching is stale data. Say a component wires a cacheable getOpenTasks method, and then the user completes a task through another Apex call. The wired list still shows the old task, because the cached result isn't updated automatically. So I call refreshApex on the wired result, or notifyRecordUpdateAvailable for record data cached by LDS. Cacheable methods can still be called imperatively, too.
points: Responses cached on the client per parameters
Use refreshApex to bust stale wired data

q: How do you call an Apex method imperatively with parameters from LWC?
alt: Pass parameters from LWC to Apex
Imperative Apex call example with async await
How do I send values to an Apex method from JavaScript?
call apex on button click lwc
a: It's a simple import-and-call. I import the method from @salesforce/apex and call it like a function, passing one object whose keys match the Apex parameter names exactly. Say the Apex method is getCases(Id accountId, String status). In JavaScript I call getCases({ accountId: this.recordId, status: 'Open' }). If I write accId instead of accountId, Apex won't get that value. It returns a promise, so I use async and await with try/catch, show a spinner while it runs, and turn the spinner off in finally. The Apex method must be static, public or global, and annotated with @AuraEnabled. Parameters can be primitives, lists, maps, sObjects, or a custom wrapper class whose fields are marked @AuraEnabled. Mismatched parameter names are a quiet bug, so I check them in review.
points: Keys in the JS object must match Apex parameter names
Returns a promise: async/await with try/catch

q: What is refreshApex and how do you use it correctly?
alt: How do I refresh wired Apex data after an update?
refreshApex not working, what am I doing wrong?
How to refresh data in LWC after DML
refresh apex example
a: refreshApex is how I fix stale wired data after a change. It re-runs a wired Apex call and bypasses the client cache, so the component shows fresh data after a change. The important detail is that I have to pass the exact provisioned value the wire gave me, not the data I copied from it. When I wire to a function, I store the whole response object in a field, say this.wiredContacts, and later call refreshApex(this.wiredContacts). For example, after a user saves a new Contact in a modal, I call refreshApex on that stored value and the list updates. It returns a promise. A common mistake, and one I look for in review, is calling refreshApex on imperatively fetched data, which does nothing. For imperative calls I just call the method again. And if other components show the same record through LDS, I also call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable.
points: Pass the original wired value, not a copy of data
Store the response when wiring to a function
Does not work for imperative calls

q: What is Lightning Data Service and why should you use it?
alt: What is LDS in LWC?
Benefits of Lightning Data Service
Why use LDS instead of Apex?
lightning data service explained
a: I'd use LDS before writing any Apex for single-record work. Lightning Data Service is the shared data layer for Lightning components. It lets me create, read, update and delete records without writing Apex, using base components like lightning-record-form or the uiRecordApi wire adapters and functions. The big advantages: it respects CRUD, field-level security and sharing automatically, it caches records on the client, and it keeps every component on the page in sync. Say a record page has my custom component and a standard component, both showing the same Account. If my component updates the Phone through LDS, the standard one refreshes too, with no extra code. I prefer LDS for single-record operations, and I use Apex when I need complex queries, many records, aggregations, or business logic that has to run on the server. Less Apex also means less code to test and maintain, which is a trade-off I'm happy to make.
points: No Apex needed for single-record CRUD
Shared client cache keeps components in sync
Use Apex for complex queries or bulk logic

q: What is the difference between lightning-record-form, lightning-record-edit-form and lightning-record-view-form?
alt: record form vs record edit form vs record view form
Which LDS form component should I use?
When would you choose lightning-record-edit-form over lightning-record-form?
difference between three record form components
a: I pick the simplest one that meets the requirement. All three use Lightning Data Service, so no Apex is needed. lightning-record-form is the quickest. You give it an object, a record Id, and fields or a layout type, and it builds a view or edit form with modes view, edit and readonly. But customization is limited. lightning-record-edit-form gives me control over the layout, because I place each lightning-input-field myself, I can add custom buttons, and I can intercept the submit to change values or validate before saving. lightning-record-view-form is the read-only version, where I place lightning-output-field components. For example, a quick Contact edit panel with standard fields is a record-form. But if the business wants a custom two-column layout, a custom button, and a status set before saving, that's record-edit-form.
points: record-form: fastest, view/edit/readonly modes, limited control
record-edit-form: custom layout with lightning-input-field, onsubmit hook
record-view-form: custom read-only layout with lightning-output-field

q: How do you set or change field values before saving in lightning-record-edit-form?
alt: Modify fields on submit in record edit form
How to add a hidden default value in lightning-record-edit-form?
Intercept save in record edit form
onsubmit prevent default record edit form
a: I'd intercept the submit. I handle the onsubmit event and call event.preventDefault() to stop the default save. Then I read event.detail.fields, add or change values, and call submit on the form with the updated fields. This is useful for values the user shouldn't type, like a parent Id or a status, or for running custom validation first. Say a component creates a Case from an Account page. The user fills in Subject and Description, and in onsubmit I add the AccountId from the page and set Status to New, then submit. After a successful save, the onsuccess event gives me the record Id, and onerror gives me the error. The form also shows errors through lightning-messages. If the rule must always hold, I also back it with a validation rule or server logic, because client-side defaults alone can be bypassed.
points: onsubmit + preventDefault, edit fields, then form.submit(fields)
code:
<lightning-record-edit-form object-api-name="Contact" onsubmit={handleSubmit} onsuccess={handleSuccess}>
    <lightning-messages></lightning-messages>
    <lightning-input-field field-name="LastName"></lightning-input-field>
    <lightning-input-field field-name="Email"></lightning-input-field>
    <lightning-button type="submit" label="Save"></lightning-button>
</lightning-record-edit-form>

handleSubmit(event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    const fields = event.detail.fields;
    fields.AccountId = this.recordId;
    this.template.querySelector('lightning-record-edit-form').submit(fields);
}
handleSuccess(event) { this.newId = event.detail.id; }

q: How do you read a record's fields in LWC without Apex?
alt: getRecord example in LWC
How to use getFieldValue?
Fetch the current record name without writing Apex
uiRecordApi getRecord
a: No Apex needed. I use the getRecord wire adapter from lightning/uiRecordApi, with the recordId and the fields I need. I import the fields from @salesforce/schema, which gives compile-time references. So if someone tries to delete a field, Salesforce knows the component depends on it. Then I use getFieldValue to read values safely, and getFieldDisplayValue for formatted values like currency or picklist labels. For example, on an Opportunity page, getFieldValue on Amount gives me the raw number for calculations, while getFieldDisplayValue gives me the formatted currency the user expects to see. Because it's LDS, it respects field-level security, it's cached, and it updates automatically when the record is edited elsewhere on the page. I also insist on schema imports over field-name strings, because that dependency tracking protects us when an admin tries to delete a field.
points: Import fields from @salesforce/schema for referential integrity
Reactive to '$recordId' and auto-updates on edit

q: How do you update a record from LWC without writing Apex?
alt: updateRecord example in LWC
Save a field change using uiRecordApi
Update record through LDS from JavaScript
update record without apex lwc
a: For a single record, I'd use the updateRecord function from lightning/uiRecordApi. I build a recordInput object with a fields map that includes the Id and the fields to change, using imported schema fields for the keys, and call updateRecord, which returns a promise. Say a button marks a Case as Escalated. The fields map has the Case Id and Status set to Escalated, and that's it, no Apex. Because it goes through Lightning Data Service, it respects security and validation rules, and every component showing that record through LDS refreshes automatically. I show a success toast when it's done, and I read the error body to show validation messages. For many records at once, I use one Apex call instead, so it's one DML statement rather than many separate requests.
points: Returns a promise; errors include validation messages
LDS cache updates all components showing the record

q: You update a record through Apex, but the standard record page and LDS components still show old values. How do you fix it?
alt: Record page not refreshing after Apex update
How do I tell LDS that a record changed on the server?
What is notifyRecordUpdateAvailable?
getRecordNotifyChange replacement
a: I'd tell LDS the record changed. LDS doesn't know about changes made in Apex, so its cache stays stale. After the Apex call succeeds, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable from lightning/uiRecordApi with the list of changed record Ids. LDS then re-fetches those records, and every wired getRecord and standard component using them updates. For example, a button calls Apex to recalculate a discount on an Opportunity. Right after it returns, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with that Opportunity Id, and the standard record details show the new value without a page reload. It replaced the older getRecordNotifyChange. If my own component got its data from a wired Apex method, I also call refreshApex on that wired result, because notifyRecordUpdateAvailable only refreshes LDS record data, not custom Apex results. Any component that saves through Apex needs this step, so it's on my review checklist.
points: Still call refreshApex for wired Apex results

q: What are the ways components can communicate with each other in LWC?
alt: How do LWC components talk to each other?
Component communication options in Lightning Web Components
Parent to child, child to parent and unrelated components communication
how to pass data between components lwc
a: I choose the mechanism based on how the components are related. Parent to child, I pass data through @api properties or call @api methods on the child. Child to parent, the child dispatches a custom event and the parent listens with an on-handler in its template. For components that aren't in the same hierarchy, like two separate components on a Lightning page, I use Lightning Message Service with a message channel, which also works across LWC, Aura and Visualforce. For example, a list component in the left column and a details component in the right column: when a user clicks a row, the list publishes the record Id on a channel and the details component picks it up. Older projects used a pub-sub module, but LMS is the supported approach now. And for record data, LDS keeps components in sync automatically. Picking the simplest option that fits keeps the codebase easy for the next developer to follow.
points: Parent to child: @api properties and methods
LDS keeps record data in sync across components

q: How do you send data from a child component to its parent?
alt: Child to parent communication example
How to fire a custom event in LWC?
How does the parent handle an event from child?
dispatch event from child lwc
a: I'd use a custom event. The child creates a CustomEvent and dispatches it, putting the data in the detail property. The event name should be lowercase, with no 'on' prefix and no spaces, for example 'select'. In the parent template I add an attribute named on plus the event name, like onselect, pointing to a handler, and the handler reads event.detail. I keep detail to primitives or a fresh copy of data, so the parent cannot accidentally mutate the child's internal state. By default the event does not bubble, which is what I want for direct child-to-parent communication. Event naming is one of the conventions I agree with the team up front, so handlers are predictable across components.

q: What do bubbles and composed mean on a custom event?
alt: Explain bubbles true composed true in LWC
Why is my event not reaching the grandparent?
Event propagation across shadow DOM
bubbles and composed flags
a: My default is both false, and anything wider needs a reason. These two flags control how far an event travels. bubbles: true lets the event move up through the DOM tree from the element that fired it. composed: true lets it cross shadow DOM boundaries, so it can escape the component's shadow root and reach ancestors in other components. With both false, the default, only the direct parent that declared the handler on the child element hears it, and that's the cleanest option. With bubbles true and composed false, it bubbles only inside the parent's template. Both true makes the event part of the component's public API to every ancestor, so I use it sparingly, because any component up the tree can start depending on it. For example, if a row inside a table needs the page to know about a click, I usually have the table catch it and re-dispatch its own event, instead of letting the row's event travel all the way up. In review, a composed event is something I always ask about, because it quietly widens the component's API.
points: Default (false/false): only the direct owner hears it

q: What is Lightning Message Service and how do you use it?
alt: Explain LMS with an example
How to communicate between components on different parts of a page?
What is a message channel?
lightning message service publish subscribe
a: Lightning Message Service is my answer for components that aren't related in the DOM. It lets them exchange messages, across LWC, Aura and Visualforce on the same Lightning page, including components in the utility bar. I create a message channel as metadata, a LightningMessageChannel file, with the fields it carries. A publisher imports the channel and MessageContext and calls publish with a payload. A subscriber calls subscribe in connectedCallback and unsubscribe in disconnectedCallback. Say an app page has a filter component on the left and a chart component on the right, with no parent-child link. When the user picks a region, the filter publishes it, and the chart reloads for that region. One gotcha: by default, subscribers only get messages in the active area. Passing APPLICATION_SCOPE makes them receive messages from anywhere in the app. I also keep a short list of the org's message channels and what each carries, so teams reuse them instead of creating near-duplicates.
points: subscribe in connectedCallback, unsubscribe on disconnect
APPLICATION_SCOPE to receive across the whole app
code:
<!-- messageChannels/RecordSelected.messageChannel-meta.xml -->
<LightningMessageChannel xmlns="http://soap.sforce.com/2006/04/metadata">
    <masterLabel>RecordSelected</masterLabel>
    <isExposed>true</isExposed>
    <lightningMessageFields><fieldName>recordId</fieldName></lightningMessageFields>
</LightningMessageChannel>

q: How does shadow DOM affect styling in LWC, and how do you style base components?
alt: Why can't my parent CSS style the child component?
How to override the style of a lightning-button?
What are styling hooks in LWC?
css not applying in lwc child
a: Styling hooks are the supported answer, and I don't let the team target internal SLDS classes. Every LWC has its own shadow tree, so its CSS is scoped. Styles in a component only apply to its own template, and a parent's styles don't leak into the child. That's why a parent can't style the inside of a child, or of a base component like lightning-button. Targeting internal SLDS classes is unsupported, because they can change, which is why it's off-limits for us. Say the design wants a lightning-button with a brand-colored background. Writing CSS against the button's inner SLDS classes isn't the way, and it can break after a release. The supported way is styling hooks, which are CSS custom properties that base components expose, and they do pass through the shadow boundary. Inside my own components, I use :host to style the component's outer element. And if a design really needs global styling, light DOM is an option for my own components.
points: CSS is scoped to the component's shadow tree
Parent styles don't reach into children

q: What is light DOM in LWC and when would you use it?
alt: Shadow DOM vs light DOM in Lightning Web Components
How do I render an LWC without shadow DOM?
When is light DOM a good idea?
lwc render mode light
a: I treat light DOM as an exception. By default an LWC renders inside a shadow tree, which isolates its markup and CSS. Light DOM renders the component's markup directly into the parent's DOM instead. I enable it by setting static renderMode = 'light' in the class and lwc:render-mode='light' on the template. It helps when global styles or a theme need to reach inside the component, when third-party libraries need normal DOM access, or for better SEO and accessibility tooling in Experience Cloud sites. For example, on an Experience Cloud site with a site-wide theme, a light DOM header component can pick up the site's fonts and colors directly. The trade-off is no encapsulation. Other code can reach in and restyle the markup, and I use this.querySelector instead of this.template.querySelector. So shadow DOM stays my default, and I use light DOM only for the components that need it. When someone wants it, I ask them to explain the reason in the pull request.

q: How do you implement infinite loading in lightning-datatable?

a: I'd combine the datatable's infinite loading with keyset paging in Apex. I set enable-infinite-loading on the datatable and handle the onloadmore event, which fires when the user scrolls near the bottom. In the handler I set event.target.isLoading to true, call Apex imperatively for the next batch, append the results as a new array, and set isLoading back to false. For paging on the server I prefer keyset paging, filtering by Id or a sort field greater than the last loaded value, because OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows. Say I load 50 Accounts at a time. q: How do you handle errors from Apex in LWC and show a meaningful message?
alt: Error handling in Lightning Web Components
Why does my LWC show 'internal server error' instead of my message?
What is AuraHandledException?
how to show apex error message in lwc
a: I'd handle it on both sides. On the Apex side, I catch exceptions and throw an AuraHandledException with a message that's safe for users. Otherwise the client may only get a generic internal error. On the client, imperative calls go in try/catch, and wired results are checked for the error property. The error shape varies. Apex errors usually have body.message, while LDS errors can have body as an array, or contain output.errors and fieldErrors. So if I only read error.body.message everywhere, an LDS save that fails a validation rule may show just a generic message, and the real field-level error gets lost. That's why I use a small reduceErrors helper that flattens all these shapes into readable strings, then show them in a toast or inline. And I log the technical details on the server, not in the UI. I'd keep one shared reduceErrors utility for the whole team, rather than every component parsing errors its own way.

q: How do you improve the performance of Lightning Web Components?
alt: LWC performance best practices
My Lightning page with custom components is slow, what would you optimize?
How to make LWC load faster?
performance tuning lwc
a: I'd measure first, and then start with data, because most slowness is server calls. I prefer LDS and cacheable wired Apex, so repeated calls hit the client cache. I select only the fields I need, and I combine several small Apex calls into one. For example, if a component makes four Apex calls on load for Account details, Contacts, Cases and counts, I'd merge them into one call that returns a wrapper. For big lists, I paginate or use infinite loading instead of loading thousands of rows. On the client, I debounce search inputs, use lwc:if so heavy child components aren't created until needed, load third-party libraries once, and keep getters and renderedCallback cheap, since they run on every render. I use stable keys in loops. And I check with browser dev tools and Apex logs rather than guess. Before a big release, I ask the team to test pages with realistic data volumes, not five sample records.
points: Fewer, leaner server calls; cacheable and LDS

q: What is the difference between Lightning Locker and Lightning Web Security?
alt: Locker Service vs LWS
What is Lightning Web Security?
Why did Salesforce introduce LWS?
locker vs lightning web security
a: LWS is the direction I'd take for any org that can switch. Both are security layers that isolate components from different namespaces, so one package can't attack another. Lightning Locker does it by wrapping global objects like window, document and DOM elements in secure proxy versions. That blocks access to other namespaces' DOM, but it also breaks a lot of third-party libraries and adds overhead. Lightning Web Security takes a newer approach. Each namespace runs in its own JavaScript sandbox, and risky APIs are modified through distortions instead of wrapped. That gives better performance, better compatibility with libraries, and lets components import modules from other namespaces. For example, if a third-party charting library keeps failing under Locker, switching the org to LWS is one of the first things I'd look at. It's turned on in Session Settings with one setting for both Lightning web components and Aura components, and new orgs have it on by default. In an older org, I'd test the switch in a sandbox first, because it affects every component at once.
points: Locker: secure wrappers around globals, strict namespace isolation
LWS: per-namespace sandboxes with API distortions
LWS: faster, more library friendly, cross-namespace imports
Enabled in Session Settings; default in new orgs

a: LDS-based components and base components enforce CRUD, FLS and sharing automatically, so that's my first choice. Apex is different, because it runs in system mode by default. So in classes called from LWC, I declare with sharing, run queries WITH USER_MODE and DML as user, or use Security.stripInaccessible when I need to remove fields gracefully. Users also need access to the Apex class through a profile or permission set. On the client, I never trust input, because anyone can call an AuraEnabled method directly. For example, hiding a Delete button for some users isn't security on its own. Someone could still call that Apex method from the browser, so the server validates everything. If I changed a record through Apex, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with the record Ids, so LDS refetches them and every component bound to that record, including standard ones, updates. For a broader refresh, Salesforce provides the RefreshView API in the lightning/refresh module, which is the LWC counterpart to force:refreshView in Aura. My component dispatches a RefreshEvent, it bubbles up to the nearest refresh container, and components that registered refresh handlers reload their data. Say a quick action recalculates an Opportunity through Apex. notifyRecordUpdateAvailable takes care of the Opportunity's own fields, and a RefreshEvent lets the other components that registered for refresh reload too. What I avoid is a full page reload with window.location, because it loses state and feels slow.
points: Containers and handlers register to take part

q: Which @salesforce scoped modules have you used in LWC?
alt: How do I get the current user Id in LWC?
How to use custom labels in Lightning Web Components?
Check a custom permission in LWC
salesforce import modules lwc
a: Scoped modules let me import platform data at compile time. The ones I use most are @salesforce/apex for Apex methods, @salesforce/schema for object and field references, @salesforce/user/Id for the current user's Id, and @salesforce/label for custom labels so text can be translated. Then @salesforce/customPermission and @salesforce/userPermission to show or hide features based on permissions, @salesforce/resourceUrl for static resources, @salesforce/messageChannel for LMS, and @salesforce/client/formFactor to adapt layouts for phone or desktop. For example, I import a custom permission like Approve_Discounts and only show the Approve button when the user has it. The button text comes from a custom label, so it can be translated without touching the code. Importing these instead of hard-coding values keeps components translatable and protected by referential integrity.

q: You need a search box that searches Accounts as the user types without calling Apex on every keystroke. How would you build it?
alt: Build an account search component with debounce
How do you debounce input in LWC?
Search as you type calling Apex in Lightning Web Components
type ahead search lwc
a: I would debounce the input. On each change I clear the previous timer and start a new one of about 300 milliseconds, and only when the user stops typing do I set the search key. The search key is a reactive parameter of a wired cacheable Apex method, so setting it triggers the call, and repeated searches come from cache. I skip the search for fewer than two characters. In Apex I bind the term in a LIKE filter, which avoids SOQL injection, enforce user mode, and limit the rows. The template shows a spinner, results, or a no-results message.
points: Bind variables in SOQL, WITH USER_MODE, LIMIT

q: Show a list of Contacts in a datatable with row actions to view, edit and delete. How would you implement it?
alt: Datatable with row actions example
How to handle onrowaction in lightning-datatable?
Add an action menu on each row of a datatable
row level actions lwc datatable
a: I add a column of type action with rowActions in typeAttributes, and handle the onrowaction event, which gives me the action name and the full row. For view and edit I use NavigationMixin to the record page with actionName view or edit. For delete I ask for confirmation with lightning/confirm, call deleteRecord from uiRecordApi, show a toast, and call refreshApex so the row disappears. The data comes from a wired cacheable Apex method, and I store the wired result so I can refresh it.

q: Give an example of parent and child components passing data both ways.
alt: Parent child communication example in LWC
Parent sends a list to child, child tells parent which one was clicked
Explain two-way communication between parent and child
parent to child and child to parent example
a: A typical example is a list and a tile. The parent loads contacts and loops over them, passing each contact into a child tile through an @api property. When the user clicks a tile, the child dispatches a custom event called select with the contact Id in detail. The parent listens with onselect, stores the selected Id, and that value can flow back down to every tile through another @api property, so the selected tile highlights itself. This keeps data ownership in the parent and the child stays reusable.
points: Parent owns state; children stay reusable
code:
<!-- parent.html -->
<template for:each={contacts} for:item="c">
    <c-contact-tile key={c.Id} contact={c} selected-id={selectedId} onselect={handleSelect}></c-contact-tile>
</template>
// parent.js
handleSelect(e) { this.selectedId = e.detail; }

// contactTile.js
@api contact;
@api selectedId;
get tileClass() { return this.contact.Id === this.selectedId ? 'tile selected' : 'tile'; }
handleClick() { this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('select', { detail: this.contact.Id })); }

q: After a user saves data through an Apex call, the list in your component still shows old values. How do you refresh it?
alt: Refreshing data after DML in LWC
Data is stale after insert, how to reload?
How to refresh wired list after imperative save?
list not updating after save lwc
a: The list is coming from a cached wired Apex method, so after an imperative save the cache is stale. I keep a reference to the wired result and, once the save promise resolves, call refreshApex on it, which re-queries the server and updates the list. If the change also affects records shown by LDS or standard components, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable with those record Ids. If the list itself was loaded imperatively, I simply call the load method again. I also show a toast and handle errors in a catch block.
points: Store the wired result; call refreshApex after save
notifyRecordUpdateAvailable for LDS and standard components

q: You need to show the Contacts of the current Account on its record page. How would you build it?
alt: Show related records of current record in LWC
How to get the recordId on a record page?
Display child records on account page with LWC
related list lwc using record id
a: I place the component on the Account record page and declare @api recordId, which the page fills in automatically. Then I wire a cacheable Apex method with accountId set to '$recordId', so it runs as soon as the Id is available. The Apex method uses with sharing and user mode and returns only the fields I need. In the template I show the records in a datatable or list, with an empty-state message. Another option without Apex is getRelatedListRecords from lightning/uiRelatedListApi, which reads a related list through LDS.
points: @api recordId is set by the record page

q: You need dependent picklists in a custom LWC form, where State depends on Country. How would you implement it?
alt: Dependent picklist in LWC with getPicklistValues
How to filter dependent picklist values in Lightning Web Components?
controllerValues and validFor explained
dependent picklist lwc without apex
a: I use the uiObjectInfoApi wire adapters. getObjectInfo gives me the default record type Id, and getPicklistValues gives me the values for each field for that record type. For the dependent field, the response includes controllerValues, which maps each controlling value to an index. Every dependent value has a validFor array listing the controlling indexes it's valid for. So say controllerValues says India is index 2. When the user picks India, I keep only the State values whose validFor includes 2, like Maharashtra or Karnataka, and drop the rest. This respects record type picklist settings and needs no Apex. If a record type is used, I pass its Id instead of the default.
points: No Apex; respects record type values

q: Two components sit in different regions of a Lightning page. When a user selects an account in one, the other must show its details. How do you connect them?
alt: Pass data between unrelated components using LMS
Communication between sibling components on a Lightning page
How to send a selected record Id to another component?
lms example sender and receiver
a: Since they have no parent-child relationship, I use Lightning Message Service. I create a message channel with a recordId field. The list component wires MessageContext and publishes the selected Id. The details component subscribes in connectedCallback, saves the Id in a field when a message arrives, and that field feeds a reactive getRecord wire or lightning-record-view-form, so it re-renders automatically. I unsubscribe in disconnectedCallback. If the publisher lives in the utility bar or another tab, I subscribe with APPLICATION_SCOPE.
points: Message channel with a recordId field
Subscriber: subscribe in connectedCallback, unsubscribe on disconnect
Feed the Id into a reactive wire

q: Users want to upload files to a Case from a custom component. How would you do it?
alt: File upload to a record in LWC
lightning-file-upload example
How to attach files to a record from LWC?
upload document to record lightning web component
a: I use the lightning-file-upload base component and set record-id to the Case Id, so uploaded files are linked to the record as Salesforce Files automatically, with no Apex. I set accept to the allowed extensions and multiple if needed. The onuploadfinished event gives me event.detail.files, with the name and document Id of each file, so I show a toast and refresh any file list I display. If I need extra processing after upload, like setting a file category, I pass the document Ids to an Apex method.
points: lightning-file-upload with record-id links files to the record
code:
<lightning-file-upload label="Attach files" name="caseFiles" record-id={recordId}
    accept={acceptedFormats} multiple onuploadfinished={handleUploadFinished}>
</lightning-file-upload>

acceptedFormats = ['.pdf', '.png', '.jpg'];
handleUploadFinished(event) {
    const files = event.detail.files;
    this.dispatchEvent(new ShowToastEvent({
        title: files.length + ' file(s) uploaded', variant: 'success'
    }));
}

q: How would you implement pagination in an LWC showing a large list of records?
alt: Pagination in Lightning Web Components
Next and previous buttons with Apex
Server-side pagination using OFFSET in LWC
paging records lwc datatable
a: I do server-side pagination, so I never load everything. The component keeps pageNumber and pageSize as reactive fields and wires a cacheable Apex method that returns one page plus the total count. Next and Previous change pageNumber, which re-runs the wire, and getters disable the buttons on the first and last page. Say there are 1,000 Cases and a page size of 25. Apex returns 25 records and a total of 1,000, so I know there are 40 pages, and on page 40 the Next button is disabled. In Apex I use LIMIT and OFFSET, which is simple, but OFFSET is capped at 2,000 rows. So for bigger data sets I switch to keyset paging, filtering by the last record's sort value, or to infinite loading.
points: Reactive pageNumber/pageSize on a cacheable wire
OFFSET max 2,000: use keyset paging for large sets

q: Your LWC works for admins but regular users see no data or an error. How do you troubleshoot it?
alt: Component works for me but not for other users
LWC shows nothing for standard users
You don't have access to the Apex class error
lwc data not visible for some profiles
a: I check access layer by layer. First, does the user's profile or permission set grant access to the Apex class? Without it, the call fails outright. Next, record visibility. If the class is with sharing, the user may simply not see those records, which is often correct. Then object and field permissions, especially if I query WITH USER_MODE, which throws when a field isn't readable. For example, if the query includes a custom Margin field that only admins can read, user mode throws for everyone else, and the component shows an error. To find the real cause, I log in as the user, check the browser console and network response for the actual error, and capture a debug log for that user. I also confirm the component is on the right Lightning page activation for their app and profile.
points: Apex class access via permission set
Sharing: record visibility differs per user
Login As, browser console, user debug log

q: Your wired Apex method never runs when the component is placed on an App page, but it works on a record page. Why?
alt: Wire not firing in LWC
recordId is undefined on app page
Why does my @wire not call Apex?
wire method not getting called
a: A wire with a reactive parameter does not call the adapter while that parameter is undefined. On a record page the framework sets recordId, but on an App page or Home page there is no record context, so '$recordId' stays undefined and the wire waits forever. The fix depends on the design: restrict the component to record pages through its targets, let the admin pass an Id as a design property, or get the Id from somewhere else like Lightning Message Service or CurrentPageReference state. Other common causes are a typo in the dollar parameter name, or the Apex method missing cacheable=true.
points: Wire waits while a reactive param is undefined
recordId only exists on record pages
Provide Id via design property, LMS or page state

q: How would you show a loading spinner and handle errors while your component fetches data?
alt: Show spinner during Apex call in LWC
Loading state in Lightning Web Components
How to display an error message when the call fails?
spinner lwc example
a: I keep a few clear states: loading, error, empty and data. Before an imperative call, I set isLoading to true, and in a finally block I set it back to false, so the spinner always goes away, even when the call fails. In the catch, I store a readable error message. For a wired call, the state is loading until either data or error is provisioned. In the template, I use lwc:if and lwc:elseif to show exactly one of these: the spinner, the error, an empty message, or the data. So if an Account has no Contacts, the user sees "No contacts found" instead of a blank box, and if the call fails, they see the reason instead of a spinner that never stops.
points: Set isLoading before, reset in finally
Store a readable error in catch
Template shows one state at a time with lwc:if

q: The business wants to see and work with tens of thousands of records in one LWC. How would you design it?
alt: Showing a very large data set in a datatable
Datatable is slow with thousands of rows
Design an LWC for big data volume
how to handle 50000 records in lwc
a: I would push back on loading everything into the browser, because a single transaction can only retrieve 50,000 rows and large payloads make the page slow. Instead I design around server-side filtering and paging: users filter first, then I load in batches with infinite loading or pagination using keyset paging. I select only the columns needed, and I show counts or summaries using aggregate queries rather than raw rows. For bulk actions on all matching records, the component sends the filter criteria to Apex and a Batch Apex or Queueable job processes them asynchronously, and the UI shows progress. If they mainly need analysis, I suggest a report or dashboard instead.
points: Filter first, then page or infinite-load in batches
Bulk actions via async Apex with progress

q: Users edit a field in the standard record detail, but your custom component on the same page keeps showing the old value. How do you fix it?
alt: Custom LWC not updating when the record is edited
Keep LWC in sync with the standard record detail
Component shows stale field after inline edit on record page
lwc not refreshing on record update
a: This happens when the component reads the record through Apex, because Apex results are cached separately and do not know the record changed. The best fix is to read record fields through Lightning Data Service, using getRecord or lightning-record-view-form, since LDS shares one cache with the standard components and updates automatically when the record is saved. If I really need Apex, for example for a calculated query, I wire getRecord on the fields that matter, and when its data changes I call refreshApex on my Apex wire. That way any edit on the page triggers a refresh.
points: Apex results don't see record edits
Prefer getRecord / record-view-form: shared LDS cache
Or watch getRecord and call refreshApex on change

q: You need one component that works on a Lightning record page and also in an Experience Cloud site. What do you consider?
alt: Reusing an LWC in Experience Cloud and internal org
LWC for both Lightning Experience and community site
What changes when an LWC runs in Experience Cloud?
lwc in experience site and lightning page
a: I add both sets of targets: the record page target, and lightningCommunity__Page plus lightningCommunity__Default, and expose the properties each one needs. Then I check context differences. External and guest users have different licenses, sharing and object access, so the Apex must be secure, with sharing and user mode. For guest users I'm extra careful, because they're unauthenticated. Say the component shows open Cases. Internally, an agent sees the Cases their sharing allows, but on the site, a customer user should only see what their own access allows, and the same Apex has to respect both. Navigation should use page references, not hard-coded URLs, since site URLs differ. Some modules behave differently in LWR sites. For example, ShowToastEvent isn't supported there, so I use lightning/toast. I also check styling against the site theme and test on mobile.
points: Targets for both record page and Experience Builder
Different licenses, sharing and guest access
Check module support in LWR sites, e.g. toasts

alt: Close quick action and refresh record page in LWC
CloseActionScreenEvent with save
How do I refresh the record after a quick action saves?
quick action lwc save and close
a: I expose the component with the lightning__RecordAction target and actionType ScreenAction. On Save I call Apex or updateRecord. If I used Apex, I call notifyRecordUpdateAvailable so the record page and related LDS components show the new values. Then I dispatch CloseActionScreenEvent to close the modal and show a success toast. On error I keep the modal open and display the message, so the user doesn't lose their input. The Cancel button just dispatches CloseActionScreenEvent.

q: Write a component that asks for confirmation and deletes the current record, then goes back to the list view.
alt: Delete record from LWC with confirmation
deleteRecord uiRecordApi example
Confirm dialog before delete in Lightning Web Components
delete and navigate to object home lwc
a: I use LightningConfirm from lightning/confirm to ask the question, which returns true or false. If confirmed, I call deleteRecord from lightning/uiRecordApi with the record Id, which goes through LDS and respects permissions. On success I show a toast and navigate to the object's list view with NavigationMixin, since the record page no longer exists. If deletion fails, for example because of a validation rule or a related record, I show the error message.
points: Navigate to standard__objectPage list after delete

q: How do you validate all inputs in a custom LWC form before saving?
alt: Form validation in Lightning Web Components
reportValidity and checkValidity example
How to check required fields in LWC before submit?
validate lightning-input fields
a: I set validation attributes on the base inputs, like required, pattern, min or type email, so each input knows its own rules. On Save I collect all inputs with querySelectorAll and reduce over them, calling reportValidity on each, which shows the error under the field and returns whether it is valid. Only if all are valid do I call Apex. For rules across fields, like end date after start date, I call setCustomValidity on the relevant input and then reportValidity. I still validate on the server too, because the client can be bypassed.

reportValidity shows messages and returns a boolean
Always validate again on the server

q: You need to show a Chart.js chart in an LWC. How do you load and use a third-party library?
alt: Use a third-party JavaScript library in LWC
loadScript from static resource example
How to include Chart.js in Lightning Web Components?
platformResourceLoader lwc
a: I upload the library as a static resource, import its URL from @salesforce/resourceUrl, and load it with loadScript from lightning/platformResourceLoader, which returns a promise and only loads the file once per page. Because the library needs a real canvas element, I load it in renderedCallback with a guard flag, then build the chart on the canvas I get through lwc:ref or querySelector. If the library manipulates DOM itself, I give it a container with lwc:dom manual. I check the library works under Lightning Web Security, and I destroy the chart in disconnectedCallback.
points: Load once in renderedCallback with a guard
Check LWS compatibility; clean up on disconnect

q: From a Contact-related component on an Account page, open the New Contact form with the Account prefilled. How?
alt: Navigate to new record page with default values
encodeDefaultFieldValues example
Prefill fields when creating a record from LWC
open new record form with account id lwc
a: I use NavigationMixin with a standard__objectPage page reference, objectApiName Contact and actionName new. To prefill fields, I build an object of field API names and values, like AccountId set to the current recordId, encode it with encodeDefaultFieldValues from lightning/pageReferenceUtils, and pass it as defaultFieldValues in the state. Salesforce opens the standard new record modal with those values, so validation rules, layouts and record types still apply.
points: Standard form keeps layouts and validation

q: What is the difference between Aura components and Lightning Web Components?
alt: Aura vs LWC
Why is LWC faster than Aura?
Compare Aura framework and Lightning Web Components
difference between aura and lwc
a: Aura is Salesforce's older, proprietary component framework. A bundle has markup, a controller, a helper, a renderer, and events defined in its own syntax. LWC is built on modern web standards, so the browser handles things like custom elements and shadow DOM natively. That makes it lighter and faster, and the code is standard JavaScript classes and modules. LWC also has better tooling, Jest unit testing, and a cleaner event model based on DOM events. For example, a simple counter in Aura means a component markup file, a controller and often a helper. In LWC it's an HTML template and one JavaScript class, plus the meta file. Both can live on the same page and share Lightning Data Service. An LWC can be placed inside an Aura component, but an Aura component can't be placed inside an LWC. For new work, Salesforce recommends LWC.
points: LWC: web standards, faster, standard JS
LWC can be nested in Aura, not the reverse
Both share LDS and coexist on a page

q: Can you use an LWC inside an Aura component, and an Aura component inside an LWC?
alt: Nest LWC in Aura
Can LWC contain Aura components?
How do Aura and LWC work together?
lwc inside aura wrapper
a: Yes, one way only. An LWC can be used inside an Aura component, and in Aura markup I reference it with the c colon camelCase name, pass values as attributes, and handle its custom events with on-handlers. An Aura component cannot be used inside an LWC, because LWC only understands web components. That is why, when migrating, we usually start with leaf components and build upward, and sometimes keep a thin Aura wrapper around an LWC when we need a capability that is only available to Aura. Both kinds of components can still communicate through Lightning Message Service and share data through LDS.
points: Aura passes attributes and listens to LWC events

q: When would you still use Aura instead of LWC today?
alt: Is Aura still needed?
What can Aura do that LWC cannot?
Should we build anything new in Aura?
use cases for aura components now
a: For new development I choose LWC by default, and Aura only when a specific feature has no LWC equivalent yet. Salesforce has been closing these gaps over the years, for example modals, console workspace tab APIs, URL-addressable components and page refresh now have LWC modules. Areas where teams have traditionally kept Aura include custom Lightning page templates for App Builder and some older integration points, like Flow local actions or the original Lightning Out beta, which needed an Aura app; Lightning Out 2.0 now runs LWCs directly. In those cases I keep the Aura part as a thin wrapper and put the real logic in an LWC inside it, so moving fully later is easy. I always confirm against current docs before deciding.
points: Default to LWC for new work
Gaps keep closing: modal, workspace API, URL addressable, refresh
Keep Aura as a thin wrapper when truly needed

q: What is the difference between component events and application events in Aura?
alt: Aura component event vs application event
When to use application events?
How do Aura events propagate?
aura events types
a: A component event is fired by a component and handled by components in its containment hierarchy, usually the parent, so it's like a child-to-parent notification. It's registered with aura:registerEvent and fired with component.getEvent, and it goes through capture and bubble phases. An application event is a broadcast. Any component with a handler for it receives it, no matter where it is on the page, and it's fired with $A.get('e.c:EventName'). Application events also have a default phase. For example, a row telling its own table "I was selected" is a component event. A message like "the selected region changed, everyone refresh" would traditionally be an application event. But because broadcasts are hard to trace and can cause performance issues, the guidance is to use component events where possible, and Lightning Message Service for cross-component communication.
points: Component event: hierarchy-based, capture and bubble
Application event: broadcast to all handlers, plus default phase
Prefer component events; LMS for unrelated components

q: How does an LWC send data to an enclosing Aura component?
alt: LWC event handled in Aura
Communicate from LWC to Aura parent
How to read event detail in Aura from LWC?
aura wrapper listen to lwc event
a: The LWC dispatches a normal CustomEvent with the data in detail. In the Aura markup, I add an attribute with on plus the event name on the LWC tag, pointing to a controller action. In the Aura controller, I read each property of detail with event.getParam and the property name. Say the LWC fires a select event with detail containing contactId. In Aura, the tag has onselect pointing to c.handleSelect, and in that handler, event.getParam('contactId') gives me the Id. Going the other way, Aura passes data to the LWC through its public @api properties as attributes, and it can call @api methods by getting the component with aura:id and component.find.
points: Aura to LWC via attributes and @api methods

q: How do you call an Apex method from an Aura component?
alt: Aura server-side controller call
$A.enqueueAction example
How to get data from Apex in Aura?
aura apex call set callback
a: I get the action with component.get('c.methodName'), set parameters with setParams using names that match the Apex parameters, and register a callback with setCallback. Inside the callback, I check response.getState(). On SUCCESS, I read getReturnValue and set it on an attribute. On ERROR, I read getError. Then I queue it with $A.enqueueAction, because Aura batches server calls. For example, to load Contacts, I get c.getContacts, set accountId with setParams, and in the callback I set the result on a contacts attribute. If I forget the enqueueAction line, the call is never sent. The Apex method must be static and @AuraEnabled, and the same method can be reused from LWC, which helps during migration.

q: What is the difference between a standard controller, a custom controller and a controller extension in Visualforce?
alt: Visualforce controller types
Standard controller vs custom controller vs extension
When do you use an extension in Visualforce?
vf page controllers explained
a: A standard controller is provided by Salesforce for an object, like standardController equals Account. It gives me the record plus actions like save, edit and delete without code, and it respects the user's permissions. A custom controller is an Apex class that completely replaces the standard one. I write all the logic myself, and it runs in system mode, so I have to handle sharing and security. An extension is an Apex class that adds to or overrides a standard or custom controller. Its constructor receives the controller, so I keep the standard save behavior and only add what's missing. For example, an Account page that needs the normal save plus a list of the Account's open Cases is a standard controller with one extension. A page can have several extensions, and if methods clash, the leftmost one wins.
points: Custom: full Apex control, system mode
Extension: adds or overrides, constructor takes the controller

q: Write a simple Visualforce controller extension for the Account standard controller.
alt: Visualforce extension example
How do you get the record in a controller extension?
ApexPages.StandardController constructor example
vf extension code
a: The extension's constructor takes ApexPages.StandardController, and from it I get the current record with getRecord or the Id with getId. I can then add properties and action methods the page calls, while the page still has the standard save and cancel actions. Here the extension loads open cases for the account and adds a custom action that returns a PageReference to redirect. I declare the class with sharing so it respects record access, and query with user mode for field security.
points: with sharing + user mode for security

q: What is view state in Visualforce and how do you fix a 'maximum view state size exceeded' error?
alt: Visualforce view state limit
How to reduce view state?
What is the transient keyword used for?
view state too large error vf
a: View state is the encrypted, hidden data Visualforce sends with a page that has an apex:form. It holds the controller's non-transient state, so it survives postbacks. The limit is 170 KB, and big lists, wrapper objects or blobs go past it quickly. Say a controller keeps a list of 2,000 wrapper rows with checkboxes. All of that travels with every postback, and you can easily hit the limit. To reduce it, I mark variables that can be rebuilt as transient so they aren't stored, query only the fields I need, avoid keeping large collections in controller state, paginate with StandardSetController, and use only one apex:form where possible. For read-heavy pages, JavaScript remoting avoids view state entirely. The View State tab in the development mode footer shows what's using the space.
points: View state holds controller state between postbacks
Paginate, fewer fields, remoting to avoid it

q: What is JavaScript remoting in Visualforce and how do you use it?
alt: @RemoteAction example
Visualforce remoting vs actionFunction
How to call Apex from JavaScript in Visualforce?
vf remoting invokeAction
a: JavaScript remoting lets JavaScript in a Visualforce page call a static Apex method annotated with @RemoteAction directly, and get the result asynchronously. It doesn't send or rebuild view state, so it's fast and good for responsive, JavaScript-heavy pages. But I have to update the page myself in the callback. I call it with Visualforce.remoting.Manager.invokeAction, passing the remote action reference, parameters, and a callback that checks event.status. For example, a type-ahead search box on a Visualforce page can call a searchAccounts remote action when the user pauses typing, and the callback draws the results list. I keep the escape option on to protect against script injection. And since the method runs in system mode, I enforce security in Apex.
points: No view state: fast, but manual DOM updates

q: What is the difference between actionFunction, actionSupport and JavaScript remoting in Visualforce?
alt: apex:actionFunction vs apex:actionSupport
When do you use remoting instead of actionFunction?
AJAX options in Visualforce
action function action support difference
a: actionSupport attaches AJAX behavior to an event on another component, like onchange on an input. It calls a controller action and rerenders part of the page. actionFunction defines a JavaScript function that calls a controller action, so I can trigger it from my own scripts, and it also supports rerender. Both submit the form and view state, run in the controller's context, and Visualforce handles the partial page refresh for me. JavaScript remoting calls a static @RemoteAction method without view state, which is faster and lighter. But the method has no access to controller instance state, and I update the page in JavaScript myself. For example, if picking a Country should refresh a State list, actionSupport on onchange is simplest. If my own script needs to call the controller after some custom logic, that's actionFunction. And for a fast search with no form state, remoting.

q: How would you approach migrating a set of Aura components to LWC?
alt: Aura to LWC migration strategy
Steps to convert Aura components into LWC
How do you plan a migration from Aura to Lightning Web Components?
aura migration best practices
a: I start with an inventory: which components exist, where they are used, how complex they are and what Aura-only features they rely on. Then I migrate bottom-up, beginning with leaf components, because an LWC can sit inside an Aura parent but not the reverse, so the app keeps working during the migration. I map concepts as I go: attributes to @api properties or fields, aura:if and aura:iteration to lwc:if and for:each, component events to custom events, application events to Lightning Message Service, $A.enqueueAction to wire or imperative Apex, and force events like showToast and navigateToSObject to their LWC modules. I reuse existing Apex, add Jest tests, and release in small batches with regression testing rather than a big-bang rewrite.

q: A business still uses several Visualforce pages. How would you modernize them, and can you use LWC inside Visualforce?

a: I first decide per page whether it needs to change at all. Pages used for PDF generation with renderAs pdf or certain email templates are still a good fit for Visualforce. Interactive pages I usually rebuild as LWCs on Lightning pages, reusing the Apex logic where it is clean and moving business rules out of controllers. If a page must stay in Visualforce for a while, I can embed an LWC in it with Lightning Out, using an Aura dependency app and $Lightning.use and createComponent, which lets me modernize piece by piece. For running LWCs on external, non-Salesforce sites, Lightning Out 2.0 is the newer generally available option.
